title.text:
Governance and
buying (practical)

objects.text: What rules must my company set for AI, and how do I question what I am sold?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 13 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 13. Last time you mapped a workflow and chose between a rule, an AI step and an agent. Today we ask what rules your company must set around that work, and how you question what you are sold. You write on your own organisation, and I show you the law and the frameworks in plain words.

I am not a lawyer, so I mark every legal point as my understanding and you confirm it with yours. So here is today’s question. What rules must my company set for AI, and how do I question what I am sold?

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you will have

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.70.png

objects.text: A risk register for your own work: each risk scored, owned and answered by a control

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.70.png

objects.text: A first draft of your acceptable use policy for AI, and five vendor due diligence questions with the answers that would worry you

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.70.png

objects.text: A plain view of the law, the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001, and the questions you take to your lawyer

slides.notes:
That question gives you four things to hold by the end. A risk register for your own work, with every risk scored and owned. A first draft of your acceptable use policy. Five due diligence questions for a vendor, each with the answer that would worry you. And a page of questions for your lawyer.

Nobody scores you. The only measure is whether your draft is clear enough for a colleague to follow on Monday.

title.text: Your two hours: 55 minutes are your own work

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_04b1f57a.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: 55 of the 120 minutes are yours: register, policy, lawyer page, vendor questions.

slides.notes:
Four things in two hours means we need a plan for the clock. Today you write the rules. After a short recall of Session 12, twenty five minutes on the ideas: the governance words, how to score a risk step by step, data classification, and the law and frameworks around them.

Then fifteen minutes taking a vendor proposal apart, including its total cost. After the break come the four practice blocks: your risk register, your policy, your page for the lawyer and your vendor questions. The last minutes are for one decision. First, a warm-up from last time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  In Session 12, how did the keyword rule and the AI compare on the twelve customer messages?
2.  Why did a person approve each draft before it went out?
3.  How do you work out hours saved?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 12. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. In Session 12, how did the keyword rule and the AI compare on the twelve customer messages? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. The keyword rule sent 7 of 12 to the right queue. The AI got 9 of 12 exact and 11 of 12 acceptable, with one wrong. The person who checks is how a wrong answer gets caught before it leaves.

Question two. Why did a person approve each draft before it went out? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. The AI sorts and drafts, and it can be wrong. The approval step catches a mistake before it leaves the company, and the result is logged.

Question three. How do you work out hours saved? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. Times a month multiplied by the minutes saved each time, divided by 60. At NVF the Monday sales email took 90 minutes and the new routine takes 10, so 80 minutes saved before review time, and 4 runs a month is 320 minutes, about 5.3 hours. After 20 minutes of review each run it is 60 minutes, or 240 minutes, 4 hours a month. Those are plan numbers, and the workbook prices review as a running cost.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet or workbook page has it. Now to today.

title.text:
How today connects: what we
already have and what it feeds

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_chain_11.90x4.45_243d3449.png
objects.alt: How today connects to the sessions before and after it

objects.text: Each session is built on the ones before it.

slides.notes:
So where does today sit in the story? The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14, and the gold one is today.

We already hold the failure modes to plan for from Session 10, risk = likelihood × impact from Session 11 and the workflow you mapped from Session 12. Nothing today starts from zero.

What today adds is this: policy, risk score L × I, total cost of ownership.

And it feeds straight into what comes next. Session 14: whether your data is ready, and a plan. Keep that chain in mind, because each idea you learn today is a step on it.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: The policies, roles and checks by which an organisation directs and controls its use of AI.
A written rule on who may use which AI tools, for what, and with what data.
A table of what could go wrong, scored by likelihood and impact, with an owner and a control.
Sorting information into levels, such as public or confidential, each with its own handling rule.
A named person who checks, approves or can stop what an AI system does.
Checking a supplier’s claims, security and contract terms before you commit.

slides.notes:
6 words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

AI governance. The policies, roles and checks by which an organisation directs and controls its use of AI.

Acceptable use policy. A written rule on who may use which AI tools, for what, and with what data.

Risk register. A table of what could go wrong, scored by likelihood and impact, with an owner and a control.

Data classification. Sorting information into levels, such as public or confidential, each with its own handling rule.

Human oversight. A named person who checks, approves or can stop what an AI system does.

Vendor due diligence. Checking a supplier’s claims, security and contract terms before you commit.

Keep those words close. The first idea uses them straight away, so let us begin.

title.text:
AI governance is the set of rules you
already use when you lend your car

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t13_bridge_11.90x4.25_ca961342.png
objects.alt: AI governance is the set of rules you already use when you lend your car

objects.text: AI governance: the policies, roles and checks by which an organisation directs and controls its AI use.

slides.notes:
Governance can sound like paperwork, so start with something you already do. When you lend your car you decide who may borrow it, you know what could go wrong, you keep the passport out of sight, you ask to be told before a long trip, you keep a logbook, and you check a garage before trusting it.

Each habit has a standard name in AI governance, which is the policies, roles and checks by which an organisation directs and controls its use of AI. The analogy breaks in one place. A car has one obvious owner, while in a company you must name who is accountable.

A policy, the first habit, is a written rule that the organisation agrees and everyone follows. Which of these habits does your company already have?

title.text:
Each limit of a model you met becomes
a rule in your acceptable use policy

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t13_bridge_11.90x4.25_a963a739.png
objects.alt: Each limit of a model you met becomes a rule in your acceptable use policy

objects.text: Left: what you learned. Right: the line it adds to your register or your policy.

slides.notes:
Now the same idea for AI. Each limit you met in the technical sessions becomes a rule. A model predicts likely words, so it can hallucinate, and a named person provides human oversight of figures and quotes. It follows text it reads, which is prompt injection, so a person approves every send and an audit log, a dated record of who or what did what, shows what happened.

Your words travel to a vendor, so data classification decides what goes in. An open weights file carries a licence. An agent holds only the permissions you give it, so you apply least privilege. And models change, so you run your evaluation set again. Which of these six worries you most?

title.text:
In my experience a ban hides AI use,
so write an acceptable use policy

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cross_0.75.png

objects.text: Ban only

runs.text: Staff still use personal accounts.
You cannot see what data leaves.
Nobody is trained or checked.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.75.png

objects.text: Policy and approved tools

runs.text: Company accounts with a named owner.
Data rules by sensitivity.
Training and one place to report.

objects.text: Shadow AI is staff using AI through personal accounts. A policy gives them a safe route.

slides.notes:
Whichever worry you picked, some leaders answer all six by banning AI. Think of a school that bans phones outright. They end up hidden in bags and used under desks. A school with a phone policy, phones away in lessons, allowed at break, handed in for tests, gets far better compliance because people can follow it.

AI is similar. In my experience a ban pushes the use out of sight. Staff keep using personal accounts, you cannot see what data leaves, and nobody is trained. That is called shadow AI. An acceptable use policy with approved tools gives people a safe route. Who in your company already uses AI through a personal account?

title.text:
Risk = likelihood × impact, as in Session
11: a register scores each from 1 to 5

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t13_scales_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Risk = likelihood × impact, as in Session 11: a register scores each from 1 to 5

objects.text: Exact chances and costs are rare, so a register scores each on a scale from 1 to 5.

runs.text: Likelihood: how probable it is, in the next 12 months.
Impact: how bad it is if it happens.
Flat tyre: likely (4), minor (2). Car stolen: rare (1), severe (5).

slides.notes:
A policy answers risks, so first we need a way to compare them. You have met the idea twice. Session 10 multiplied the chance of an error by its cost in shillings, and Session 11 called the same product risk: likelihood times impact. What changes today is the units.

Exact chances and shilling costs are rare, so the Risk Register template scores each on a scale from one to five, with words so that two people score alike: one is rare, five is almost certain; one is a few minutes of rework, five is serious harm or legal action.

Back to the car, where a flat tyre and a stolen car are both risks, things that could go wrong. A flat tyre is likely, four, within the next twelve months, but minor, two. A stolen car is rare, one, but severe, five. Which one worries you more?

title.text:
Multiply the two to rank risks:
a flat tyre scores 4 × 2 = 8

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t13_riskgrid_7.70x4.80_59e7b389.png
objects.alt: Multiply the two to rank risks: a flat tyre scores 4 × 2 = 8

objects.text: Risk score = likelihood × impact, from 1 to 25.

runs.text: R = L × I: R the risk score, L likelihood, I impact.
High 15 to 25, Medium 8 to 14, Low 1 to 7.

slides.notes:
To rank them, multiply, exactly as in Session 11. The flat tyre is four times two, eight. The stolen car is one times five, five. As before, a risk matters when it is both fairly likely and fairly bad, so a one on either scale keeps the product small.

The smallest score is one times one, one; the largest is five times five, twenty five. The grid shows every product. In symbols the risk score R equals L times I, likelihood times impact; this grid is what industry calls a risk matrix. The template turns the score into a level: High from fifteen, which needs a control and a report to the Managing Director; Medium from eight to fourteen; Low below eight, accept and watch.

So the tyre is Medium. What would you do about it?

title.text:
A risk register writes each risk as one row:
score, owner, control and the risk left after it

rows.text: A spare tyre in the boot
Approved tools only; a data table in the policy

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_lock_0.50.png

objects.text: Control: an action that lowers the likelihood or the impact. Residual risk: the level left after the control.

slides.notes:
That question is the control. A control is an action that lowers the likelihood or the impact. A spare tyre in the boot does not stop punctures, but it cuts the impact from two to one, so the risk left afterwards, the residual risk, is four times one, four, Low.

A risk register is simply a table with one row for each risk: the score and level, one named owner who answers for it, the control, and the residual risk. The second row is from the template, for AI: data leakage, staff pasting customer data into a free AI account.

Three times five is fifteen, High, owned by the Managing Director, controlled by approved tools, leaving Medium. Now the other typical AI risks.

title.text:
The eight typical AI risks of the
template, placed on the same grid

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t13_riskgrid_7.70x4.80_e80db856.png
objects.alt: The eight typical AI risks of the template, placed on the same grid

objects.text: Three are High, five Medium. Each needs a control.

runs.text: Wrong answer: 4 × 4 = 16, High.
Broad permission: 3 × 5 = 15, High.
Cost runaway: 3 × 3 = 9, Medium.

slides.notes:
Here are the eight grey rows of the Risk Register template, scored the same way. Most come from failures you saw in the course. A wrong answer, the hallucination of Session 10, is likely, four, and major, four: sixteen, High. Broad permission, an assistant given full access to a mailbox, is three times five, fifteen, High, like data leakage.

Prompt injection and bias are three times four, twelve, Medium. Cost runaway, a loop that keeps calling a paid service, is three times three, nine, Medium, and so is vendor lock-in, data you cannot move to another supplier. When only one person knows the set-up, four times three is twelve.

These are example scores; in the practice block you score your own. Which of these would sit higher in your company?

title.text:
Data classification: four questions
tell staff what may go into an AI tool

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t13_dataflow_7.70x4.80_797da5e8.png
objects.alt: Data classification: four questions tell staff what may go into an AI tool

objects.text: Like papers at home: the passport locked away, the flyer on the fridge. The strictest answer wins.

runs.text: Payroll is Confidential and Personal: use the stricter rule.
When unsure, treat the data as one level more sensitive.

slides.notes:
Data leakage scored High, so here is the rule that guards against it. At home you keep a passport in a locked drawer, a phone bill in a tray and a flyer on the fridge. Data classification does the same: it sorts information into levels by the harm a leak would cause, and gives each level a handling rule.

This is section 4 of the AI Use Policy template. Staff ask four questions in order. Does it name a living person?

Then it is personal data, which my understanding of Uganda’s Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2019 describes as information from which a person can be identified. Would it harm us if it leaked?

Confidential. Staff only?

Internal. Published?

Public. The strictest answer wins. Which of your information lands in the top box?

title.text:
One handbook clause is a start, and an
acceptable use policy finishes the job

objects.text: Nile Valley Foods staff handbook, version 4, clause 4.4. The company and the handbook are fictional.
The clause
“Staff must not paste customer personal data, price lists or contracts into a public AI tool or website unless the Managing Director has approved that tool in writing.”
What it settles
Three kinds of data stay out of public tools, and one person approves a tool in writing.
What it leaves open
Which tools are approved, who checks the result, what is kept on record, and what to do after a mistake.

slides.notes:
A picture of four questions is helpful, and yet many companies start with something much shorter. Here is a real clause from the fictional NVF handbook. Clause 4.4 says staff must not paste customer personal data, price lists or contracts into a public AI tool unless the Managing Director has approved that tool in writing. That settles a lot. Three kinds of data stay out, and one person approves.

But it leaves the practical questions open. Which tools are approved?

Who checks the result?

What do we keep on record?

What happens after a mistake?

Your policy answers those. Read your own staff rules for AI. Which questions do they leave open?

title.text:
Four layers of rules sit around
your AI use, and only one is yours

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t13_layers_11.90x4.25_5d46359f.png
objects.alt: Four layers of rules sit around your AI use, and only one is yours

objects.text: My understanding, and not legal advice. Your lawyer confirms what binds you.

slides.notes:
Your policy does not stand alone, so let me place it among the other rules around you. Think of four layers. The outer layer is the law, and it binds you whether you like it or not. In Uganda the one I would name first is the Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2019, because it covers personal data. Next are standards such as ISO/IEC 42001, which an auditor can certify.

Then guides such as the NIST framework, the OECD principles and the African Union strategy, which are voluntary and free to copy from. The inner layer is yours: the policy your people follow on Monday. I am not a lawyer, so confirm the outer layer with yours.

title.text:
My understanding: the 2019 Act puts
duties on personal data in AI tools

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_icons_7.70x4.80_20a55f4f.png
objects.alt: My understanding: the 2019 Act puts duties on personal data in AI tools

objects.text: Personal data in an AI tool brings duties.

runs.text: I read the Act on ULII.
I found no AI-only statute. Reports said a national AI strategy was still in draft in mid-2026.

slides.notes:
The outer layer binds you, so I read the Act itself on ULII, the Uganda Legal Information Institute. Four points matter for AI tools. Section nineteen: if a Ugandan company sends personal data abroad, the other country needs protection at least equal to the Act, or the person must have consented. A cloud AI tool often means data abroad. Sections twenty and twenty one: take reasonable security measures, and make processors, firms such as an AI vendor that handle the data for you, promise the same in the contract.

Section twenty three: tell the Authority, in my reading the regulator whose Personal Data Protection Office handles this, immediately of unauthorised access. Section twenty nine: a register. This is my understanding. Which duties apply to you is a question for your lawyer. The Act is only one voice, because vendors will quote others at you.

title.text:
Five names you will hear,
and what you do with each

rows.text: Voluntary US framework (National Institute of Standards and Technology), 2023: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
A 2023 standard for an AI management system that can be certified
Ask a vendor whether it holds it
Adopted in 2019 and updated in May 2024: five values
Endorsed by the AU Executive Council in July 2024
EU law. It can reach firms outside the EU when their AI output is used there
Ask your lawyer if you sell in the EU

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_stamp_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_flag_0.50.png
/Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_doc_0.50.png

objects.text: Dates and rules change. My understanding is that the EU dates were revised in 2026. Check before you rely on them.

slides.notes:
Those were the law; now the names that vendors bring to the meeting. Five names you will hear. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework, from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, is voluntary, with four functions: govern, map, measure and manage. Use it as a checklist. ISO/IEC 42001, from the International Organization for Standardization and the International Electrotechnical Commission, is a standard for an AI management system, and a vendor can be certified against it, so ask. Like a food safety certificate on a restaurant wall, it speaks about the system and says little about each dish.

OECD principles: 2019, updated 2024. African Union strategy: July 2024. The EU AI Act can reach firms outside Europe when their AI output is used there, and its dates were revised in 2026. Ask your lawyer if you sell into the EU. Now a proposal that hides behind such names.

title.text:
Demonstration: read the OrbitDesk
proposal and mark what you cannot check

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t13_redflags_7.30x3.90_cb726837.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: read the OrbitDesk proposal and mark what you cannot check

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: A claim with no number, source or limit.
What the vendor asks you to share or sign.
What the proposal leaves out.

slides.notes:
Let me put all of this to work on a real looking pitch. This is the OrbitDesk proposal, an invented vendor pitching an autonomous finance agent to NVF. Read it with me, section by section, and watch for the lines you could not check. I mark each one. Section three promises accuracy with no number. Section four lets the agent pay with no approval up to the full bank balance.

Section five lets customer inputs improve their models. There are no references, no cap on usage, no exit, a deadline, and a request for your bank login. Which line would have worried you first? Notice that each one connects to something from the technical sessions.

title.text:
Two fresh AI reviews each
caught all 11 planted red flags

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_catch_11.90x4.25_4d743027.png
objects.alt: Two fresh AI reviews each caught all 11 planted red flags

objects.text: Recorded runs: Claude, two fresh sessions, 4 Nov 2026. Not ChatGPT or Gemini. A blunt proposal.

slides.notes:
You have picked out the lines yourself, so now compare them with what two AI reviewers made of the same pages. The course writers planted eleven red flags on purpose and listed them in an answer key. I gave two fresh AI sessions only the proposal and the request: review it, list red flags, give eight questions. The key stayed hidden. Both runs caught all eleven planted red flags, and both found extras, such as the minimum commitment of thirty six months of fees.

Both runs also flagged the request for bank login details. This is a recorded run of Claude, from 4 November 2026. Another product or another day may differ. The proposal is deliberately blunt. What would a quieter proposal look like?

title.text:
The AI review helped, and
you still do the checking

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.75.png

objects.text: In these two runs

runs.text: All 11 red flags, both times
Eight questions each
A read-only pilot as the next step

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_flag_0.75.png

objects.text: What you still do

runs.text: Check its quotes: run 2 quoted two phrases that are not there
Judge the vendor’s answers
Test claims on your data

objects.text: Use the AI as a second reader. You make the final call.

slides.notes:
Eleven out of eleven might tempt you to hand the whole job to the AI, so here is what it still leaves to you. The AI was a useful second reader. It found everything planted, wrote sensible questions and suggested a read-only pilot with a person approving every payment. But look at what you still do. Run two quoted two phrases that are not in the proposal. One was tens of thousands of invoices and the other was sign now.

A confident quote can be wrong, which is the failure from Session 10. So check quotes against the page, judge the vendor’s answers yourself, and test claims on your own data. One check needs only a calculator.

title.text:
Total cost of ownership: a free phone on a
24-month plan still costs UGX 2,400,000

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t13_tco_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Total cost of ownership: a free phone on a 24-month plan still costs UGX 2,400,000

objects.text: Total cost of ownership (TCO): everything you commit to pay over the term.

runs.text: TCO = set-up + months × monthly fee, plus usage.

slides.notes:
That calculator check is easiest to learn in a phone shop. The phone is free today, on a twenty-four-month plan at UGX 100,000 a month. What do you really commit to?

The set-up is zero. The fees are twenty four months times 100,000, which is 2,400,000. So the total is zero plus 2,400,000, UGX 2,400,000, before any extra data bundles, which you pay by use. That total is the total cost of ownership, TCO: everything you commit to pay over the term.

In words, TCO equals the set-up cost plus the number of months times the monthly fee, plus any usage charges on top. Now the same sum on the OrbitDesk proposal.

title.text:
Read the commercial terms with a
calculator: 36 months is at least USD 86,400

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t13_contract_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Read the commercial terms with a calculator: 36 months is at least USD 86,400

objects.text: The proposal’s own numbers give the least you commit to.

runs.text: TCO = 0 + 72,000 + 14,400 = USD 86,400, before usage.
Usage: USD 0.40 an action, no cap.

slides.notes:
OrbitDesk works like the phone, in US dollars. The platform fee is USD 2,400 a month for an initial term of thirty six months, and set-up is included, so zero. Thirty six times 2,400 in two easy parts: thirty six times 2,000 is 72,000, and thirty six times 400 is 14,400.

Add them: USD 86,400 at least, before any usage. Then it renews each year at a rate nobody states. Usage above the plan costs forty cents an action, an action being one task the agent performs, with no monthly cap, and nobody defines an action. If an agent loops a thousand times, that is USD 400 more, and the bill has no ceiling: the cost runaway row of your register.

Which term would you negotiate first?

title.text:
Vendor due diligence: after the review, five
steps keep you in control of a purchase

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_634d0037.png
objects.alt: Vendor due diligence: after the review, five steps keep you in control of a purchase

objects.text: On the Vendor Question List, a 0 in data and privacy, security, or contract and exit is a reason to stop.

slides.notes:
You have found the problems, so what do you do with them before anyone signs? This is vendor due diligence: checking a supplier before you commit, like asking for the service history of a used car and taking a test drive. Send your questions in writing. Score each answer zero, one or two on the Vendor Question List, thirty questions in six groups. Ask for proof, such as an audit report and two customers you can call. Then run a pilot: your own data, a baseline from your workflow map, a person approving every action, and a stop rule written first.

Sign only with an exit clause, a data export and a cap on costs. A zero in data and privacy, security, or contract and exit is a reason to stop.

title.text: Practice: score the risks of your own work

objects.text: 15 minutes
Hands-on, on your own work
Edit the Risk Register for your own work.

runs.text: Open Risk Register.xlsx. Edit the eight grey rows for your own work.
Score Likelihood and Impact from 1 to 5. The sheet works out Score and Level.
Name an Owner and write a Control for your top five.
Add one risk of your own, such as over-reliance.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_0028ffe4.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: A register with five scored risks, each with an owner and a control.

slides.notes:
Now the vendor waits, and it is time for you to write, starting with the register we scored early on. You have fifteen minutes, and I walk round while you work. Open the Risk Register. The eight grey rows are typical AI risks. Edit them for your own work. Start with what you saw fail in the course: made up facts, hidden instructions, data leaving, an agent with too much access. Score likelihood and impact from one to five and let the sheet work out the score and level.

Then name one owner for each and write a control, a real action that lowers the risk. Do your top five. Finish the rest after class. Tell me which row you scored High.

title.text: Practice: write your acceptable use policy

objects.text: 15 minutes
Hands-on, on your own work
Draft six sections of the AI Use Policy Template.

runs.text: Section 3: list approved tools, each with a plan and an owner.
Section 4: fill the data classification table with the four questions from the slide.
Section 5: list what always needs human oversight, a named reviewer.
Sections 7, 8 and 10: owner, incident contact and time, review date.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_5.50x3.55_64f0e1d3.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: Sections 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 10 of your policy draft.

slides.notes:
Your register says what to guard against, so the next page tells staff how. Again you have fifteen minutes, and I walk round. Open the AI Use Policy template. It has eleven sections, and you write six today. Section three: the approved tools, each with a plan and an owner. Section four: the data table, using the four questions. Section five: what always needs a named reviewer, such as payments, contracts and hiring.

Sections seven, eight and ten: who owns each tool, who hears about an incident and how fast, and the review date. Replace every square bracket with your own words. Sections one, two, six, nine and eleven can wait until after class.

title.text:
Practice: put your questions
to the law and name an owner

objects.text: 10 minutes
Hands-on, on your own work
Prepare the page you take to your lawyer.

runs.text: In the AI Use Policy Template find the list Questions to take to my lawyer.
Mark which of your AI uses involve personal data.
Write the date you will see your lawyer.
Name the policy owner, a deputy and the review date.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_5.50x3.55_0262beca.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: A lawyer page with your uses marked, a date, and a named owner and deputy.

slides.notes:
Your data rules depend on the law, so this block is for your lawyer. You have ten minutes, and I walk round. The template ends with five questions to take to your lawyer. Which of our AI uses involve personal data?

What are our duties under the 2019 Act for each use?

Whether and when must we report a breach?

What must a vendor contract say about our data?

What must we tell staff and customers?

Mark which of your own AI uses involve personal data, write the date you will see your lawyer, and name the policy owner and a deputy so the policy does not stall when one person is away.

title.text:
Practice: vendor due diligence
on one tool, five questions

objects.text: 15 minutes
Hands-on, on your own work
Use the Vendor Question List on one tool you use, trial or were pitched.

runs.text: Pick one tool. Open Vendor Question List.xlsx, sheet Questions.
Answer the data, security and exit groups. Score 0, 1 or 2. A silence scores 0.
Choose the five questions that matter most for your work.
Write the answer that would worry you next to each.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_a8a64fb8.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: Three gaps in what you know, and five questions with red-flag answers.

slides.notes:
With the law page ready, the last block looks outward at a tool someone is selling you. You have fifteen minutes, and I walk round. Pick one tool that your company uses, is trialling or was pitched. Open the Vendor Question List. It has thirty questions in six groups, and the column Red-flag answers shows what a worrying reply looks like. Answer the data and privacy, security, and contract and exit groups from what you know today.

Where you do not know, leave it blank, because a silence scores zero. Then choose the five questions that matter most for your work and write the answer that would worry you. These go to the vendor in writing.

title.text:
Decision: what do you do
with the next AI proposal?

objects.text: A vendor sends you a proposal tomorrow. Which route do you take?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cross_0.80.png

objects.text: Decline
A red flag on payments, bank access or your data with no fix. Stop here.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_mail_0.80.png

objects.text: Ask in writing
Send your five questions, score the answers, and decide when you have them.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_clock_0.80.png

objects.text: Run a pilot
Small, your data, a baseline, a person approving every action and a stop rule.
Write the route, the reason and the first step in your workbook.

slides.notes:
You now hold a register, a policy draft, a lawyer page and vendor questions, so let us use them on a case. Think of the tool you questioned a moment ago. Decision time. A vendor sends you a proposal tomorrow. You have three routes. Decline, when a red flag on payments, bank access or your data has no fix. Ask in writing, when the proposal is promising but silent: send your five questions, score the answers and decide when you have them.

Or run a pilot, when the answers are good: small scope, your own data, a baseline, a person approving every action and a stop rule written first. Which route do you take, and what is the first step? Write it down.

title.text:
Take the policy draft and the
questions home, and book your lawyer

objects.text: What you keep from today

runs.text: Your Risk Register, your AI Use Policy draft, your Vendor Question List with five questions, and your page of questions for the lawyer.

objects.text: Our question today
What rules must my company set for AI, and how do I question what I am sold?
Next session
Session 14: data readiness, roadmap and 90-day plan. Optional: list where your organisation keeps its information.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_4.10x4.50_3ec4adfa.png

slides.notes:
Whichever route you chose, your drafts are what you rely on next. The policy is a first draft, so share it with one colleague and your lawyer before anyone signs it. Keep the vendor questions ready for the next proposal that lands on your desk. If a question stayed open today, write it on the lawyer page.

Your rules are only as good as the information they protect, and that is the subject of Session 14, the last one. If you can, list the places where your organisation keeps its information before then.

We began with this question: What rules must my company set for AI, and how do I question what I am sold? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
